articles.description: One coding agent is a productivity tool. Two agents in the same repository is a sociology experiment....
articles.body_html:
Three Agents, One Repo: The Coordination Problem Nobody Designed For

One coding agent is a productivity tool. Two agents in the same repository is a sociology experiment. Three is a coordination problem that most teams solve for the first time in production, on a Friday.

The infrastructure conversation covers fleet orchestration and control planes. It skips the boring, decisive question: what happens when two agents touch the same file at the same time, and who resolves what they did to each other?

The Three Collisions

The mechanical collision is the friendly one. Two agents edit the same lines, git refuses to merge, and the failure is loud. Everyone notices. This is the good case, because the system said no.

The semantic collision is the dangerous one. Agent A changes the meaning of a function's return value. Agent B, working from the old contract, builds a feature that reads it. The merge is clean. The tests each wrote still pass in isolation. The system now believes two incompatible things, and nothing failed anywhere.

The duplicate collision is the expensive one. Two agents, given overlapping tickets, build the same feature twice with different names. Both PRs look competent. One of them is pure waste, and until someone notices, both are load.

None of these are exotic. They are the exact failure modes human teams have, at a speed that breaks the human mechanisms we built to catch them.

The Human Mechanism We Forgot to Port

Human teams coordinate through standups, hallway conversations, and ownership maps. "I'm touching the auth module, don't start there." It is informal, inefficient, and it works.

Agents attend no standup. They hold no grudges, share no memory, and read no hallway. The coordination layer has to become explicit, which means it has to become infrastructure:

A claim queue. Work is assigned or claimed, and a claim is visible. No two agents start the same ticket because the ticket said who started it. This is a work queue, not a scheduler, and it can be a spreadsheet before it is a platform.

An ownership map. Which files, modules, and decisions belong to which stream of work. Agents respect boundaries they are told about. They cannot respect boundaries nobody wrote down.

A merge gate between agents. Agent PRs that touch adjacent areas wait for the earlier one to land. Serializing the hot paths costs throughput and buys correctness, which is a trade humans already make every day.

A human integration owner. When agent PRs collide, a person who owns the integration decides. Not because humans are faster. Because someone has to be accountable for the seam, and accountability does not delegate to a process.

💡 Pro-tip: the semantic collision is the one to design against first. The mechanical one announces itself. The semantic one ships clean, passes its own tests, and gets discovered by a customer. A shared contract check between agents working in the same area is worth more than any lock.

Where This Breaks Down

Two or three agents on one repo is not a fleet, and the interesting failures will not always reproduce on demand. Solo developers with a single agent can skip all of this. The problem arrives the first time someone parallelizes "funnel all the open tickets to the agents" without anyone asking which tickets share a codepath.

There is also a real risk of over-engineering: most teams need a claim queue and a merge order, not a control plane, on day one.

But the direction of travel is obvious. The team now includes non-human contributors, and every org-design problem humans ever had, multiplied by speed and stripped of social instinct, is coming to a repository near you.

How many agents touch your repo before the first collision, and who resolved it? Was it loud, or was it clean?

References

  1. The fleet-level version of this problem, and why agent fleets need a control plane: Kubernetes for Agents
  2. The gatekeeper pattern for what agents may do when they get there: I Stopped Trusting AI Agents With Tools. So I Built a Gatekeeper.

articles.title: Keyboard Accessibility Testing with Playwright: Modals, Menus, Tabs and the Bugs axe-core Misses
articles.description: I built a small “Account settings” page with four everyday components: a clickable div that saves the...
articles.body_html:
I built a small “Account settings” page with four everyday components: a clickable div that saves the profile, a delete-account modal, an “Export as” menu button and a set of notification tabs. Then I broke their keyboard accessibility in thirteen ways that I see in real code reviews: outline: none, a positive tabindex, a dropdown hidden with opacity: 0, a keydown handler that swallows Tab, and so on.

axe-core 4.14, run with WCAG 2.2 AA and best-practice rules, flagged one of those thirteen. A Playwright suite that actually presses Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, arrow keys and Escape failed on all of them, 19 out of 19 tests.

That gap is the point of this article. Automated rule engines read the DOM; keyboard accessibility is about behavior over time: where focus goes after a key press, whether it can leave, whether you can see it. The axe-core README itself says axe finds “on average 57% of WCAG issues automatically”, and the WebAIM Million 2026 report reminds that “not all conformance failures can be automatically detected.”

If you already run an accessibility audit with axe on whole pages, this is the next layer: keyboard accessibility testing at the component level. We will:

  • Write down the keyboard contract for each component from the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG).
  • Build the broken version and the fixed version of each component.
  • Encode the contract as Playwright tests that check document.activeElement, :focus-visible and what is covering the focused element.
  • Run axe-core against the broken page and compare.

Stack: @playwright/test 1.63.0 (Chromium 153), axe-core 4.14.0, @axe-core/playwright 4.14.0, plain HTML and JavaScript, no framework. All terminal output below is copied from real runs.

Keyboard accessibility in WCAG 2.2: five criteria

Keyboard navigation accessibility in WCAG 2.2 comes down to five success criteria, starting with WCAG 2.1.1 Keyboard. The wording below is quoted from the W3C Recommendation:

Criterion Level What it requires How we test it
2.1.1 Keyboard A “All functionality of the content is operable through a keyboard interface” Every action is reachable and fires on Enter/Space/arrows
2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap A Focus “can be moved away from that component using only a keyboard interface” Tab and Shift+Tab can walk the whole page
2.4.3 Focus Order A Components receive focus “in an order that preserves meaning and operability” Recorded Tab sequence equals the visual order; modal keeps focus inside
2.4.7 Focus Visible AA “the keyboard focus indicator is visible” Focused element is visible and has an outline or box-shadow
2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) AA The focused component “is not entirely hidden due to author-created content” Hit-test the focused element under a sticky banner

2.4.11 is new in WCAG 2.2, which became a W3C Recommendation on 5 October 2023 (the current dated edition is from 12 December 2024). Its siblings 2.4.12 and 2.4.13 are AAA and out of scope here.

The keyboard accessibility WCAG criteria say nothing about arrow keys inside tabs, Escape in a menu, or where focus lands after a modal closes. Those conventions come from the ARIA Authoring Practices. The tests below encode them too.

The keyboard contract for each component

Before writing any code, I turn the APG patterns into a short contract per component. This is the spec the tests check.

Cheat sheet of the keyboard contract for button, modal dialog, menu button and tabs: which key does what, and where focus must land

The rules that cause the most bugs:

  • Composite widgets are one Tab stop. APG’s keyboard interface guide says the tab sequence “should include only one focusable element of a composite UI component”. Inside a tablist or menu, arrow keys move focus, not Tab.
  • A modal moves focus in and gives it back. On open, focus goes inside the dialog. On close, it returns to the element that opened it.
  • Escape closes things. Dialogs, menus and popups.
  • Focus is never lost. APG explicitly warns against focus falling back to body after a dialog closes or an item is deleted.

Step 1. Test helpers: where is focus, and can I see it?

Every keyboard test asks one of four questions. I put them in a fixture file so each spec stays readable. The variant option lets the same tests run against bad.html and good.html.

exports.test = base.test.extend({
  variant: ['good', { option: true }],
  page: async ({ page, variant }, use) => {
    await page.goto('file://' + path.resolve(__dirname, `../site/${variant}.html`));
    await use(page);
  },
});
exports.expect = base.expect;

/** Short description of document.activeElement: "button#save", "body", ... */
exports.focused = page => page.evaluate(() => {
  const el = document.activeElement;
  return el ? el.tagName.toLowerCase() + (el.id ? '#' + el.id : '') : 'null';
});

/** Press Tab n times and record where focus lands after each press. */
exports.tabWalk = async (page, n, key = 'Tab') => {
  const stops = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    await page.keyboard.press(key);
    stops.push(await exports.focused(page));
  }
  return stops;
};

/** Is there any visible indicator on the focused element? outline or box-shadow. */
exports.focusIndicator = page => page.evaluate(() => {
  const el = document.activeElement;
  const s = getComputedStyle(el);
  const outline = s.outlineStyle !== 'none' && parseFloat(s.outlineWidth) > 0;
  const shadow = s.boxShadow !== 'none';
  const visible = el.checkVisibility({ opacityProperty: true, visibilityProperty: true });
  return { focusVisible: el.matches(':focus-visible'), indicator: outline || shadow, elementVisible: visible };
});

/** WCAG 2.4.11: is the focused element entirely covered by something else? */
exports.entirelyObscured = page => page.evaluate(() => {
  const el = document.activeElement;
  const r = el.getBoundingClientRect();
  const pts = [[0.5, 0.5], [0.1, 0.1], [0.9, 0.1], [0.1, 0.9], [0.9, 0.9]]
    .map(([fx, fy]) => [r.left + r.width * fx, r.top + r.height * fy]);
  return pts.every(([x, y]) => {
    const top = document.elementFromPoint(x, y);
    return !top || !(el === top || el.contains(top));
  });
});

Notes on the helpers:

  • tabWalk uses Playwright’s keyboard API, which dispatches keydown and keyup, so the same key handlers run as for a real key press.
  • focusIndicator checks two things separately. el.matches(':focus-visible') tells you the browser wants to show focus. Whether anything is actually drawn is a different question, so it also reads the computed outline and box-shadow, and calls checkVisibility({ opacityProperty: true }) to catch focusable elements that are invisible.
  • entirelyObscured samples five points of the focused element with elementFromPoint. If every point hits something else, the element is treated as entirely hidden, a practical approximation of the 2.4.11 failure condition.

The project config runs the same spec twice:

// @ts-check
const { defineConfig } = require('@playwright/test');

module.exports = defineConfig({
  testDir: './tests',
  reporter: [['list']],
  expect: { timeout: 2000 },
  workers: 2,
  use: { browserName: 'chromium', viewport: { width: 1000, height: 700 } },
  projects: [
    { name: 'bad', testMatch: 'keyboard.spec.js', use: { variant: 'bad' } },
    { name: 'good', testMatch: 'keyboard.spec.js', use: { variant: 'good' } },
    { name: 'native', testMatch: 'native-dialog.spec.js' },
  ],
});

Step 2. Page-level checks: Tab order, traps, visible focus, obscured focus

These four tests cover 2.1.2, 2.4.3, 2.4.7 and 2.4.11 for the whole page.

test.describe('page-level keyboard checks', () => {
  test('2.4.3 Tab order follows the visual order', async ({ page }) => {
    expect(await tabWalk(page, 8)).toEqual([
      'button#save', 'button#open-modal', 'button#menu-trigger', 'button#t-email',
      'div#p-email', 'input#email', 'a#privacy', 'a#cookie-settings',
    ]);
  });

  test('2.1.2 Tab and Shift+Tab can leave every component', async ({ page }) => {
    const forward = await tabWalk(page, 12);
    expect(forward).toContain('a#cookie-settings');           // reached the last control
    await page.locator('#cookie-settings').focus();
    const back = await tabWalk(page, 12, 'Shift+Tab');
    expect(back).toContain('button#save');                    // and walked back to the first
  });

  test('2.4.7 every Tab stop has a visible focus indicator', async ({ page }) => {
    const failures = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
      await page.keyboard.press('Tab');
      const f = await focusIndicator(page);
      if (!f.indicator || !f.elementVisible) failures.push({ el: await focused(page), ...f });
    }
    expect(failures).toEqual([]);
  });

  test('2.4.11 focused controls are not hidden behind the cookie bar', async ({ page }) => {
    const hidden = [];
    for (const id of ['#email', '#privacy']) {
      await page.locator(id).focus();                         // focus() scrolls it into view
      if (await entirelyObscured(page)) hidden.push(id);
    }
    expect(hidden).toEqual([]);
  });
});

Here is what the broken page did. The first test records where eight Tab presses land:

1) [bad] › page-level keyboard checks › 2.4.3 Tab order follows the visual order
Error: expect(received).toEqual(expected) // deep equality
- Expected  - 7
+ Received  + 7
  Array [
-   "button#save",
-   "button#open-modal",
-   "button#menu-trigger",
-   "button#t-email",
-   "div#p-email",
    "input#email",
-   "a#privacy",
-   "a#cookie-settings",
+   "button#open-modal",
+   "a#csv",
+   "a#json",
+   "a#pdf",
+   "li",
+   "li",
+   "li",
  ]

Every line of that diff is a separate bug:

  • input#email comes first because it has tabindex="1", although it sits in the footer. WebAIM’s advice is blunt: do not use tabindex values of 1 or greater.
  • div#save and the “Export as” div never appear: they are not focusable at all.
  • a#csv, a#json, a#pdf receive focus while the menu is closed. The dropdown was hidden with opacity: 0, which hides pixels, not focusability.
  • li, li, li is the same element three times. Focus entered the first tab and never left.

Recorded Tab sequence on the fixed page versus the broken page: the broken page jumps to the footer, focuses three invisible menu links and then gets stuck on the first tab

That last one is a keyboard trap (2.1.2), and it came from code that looks harmless:

// "Make Enter work too" -- but preventDefault() runs for every key, Tab included
tab.addEventListener('keydown', e => {
  e.preventDefault();
  if (e.key === 'Enter') select(tab);
});

A mouse user never notices. A keyboard user is stuck on the first tab of the page with no way forward or back.

The focus-indicator test reported each stop. focusVisible: true with indicator: false is the signature of *:focus { outline: none; }: the browser decided to show focus and the CSS erased it.

3) [bad] › page-level keyboard checks › 2.4.7 every Tab stop has a visible focus indicator
Error: expect(received).toEqual(expected) // deep equality
- Expected  -  1
+ Received  + 50
- Array []
+ Array [
+   Object {
+     "el": "input#email",
+     "elementVisible": true,
+     "focusVisible": true,
+     "indicator": false,
+   },
+   Object {
+     "el": "button#open-modal",
+     "elementVisible": true,
+     "focusVisible": true,
+     "indicator": false,
+   },
+   Object {
+     "el": "a#csv",
+     "elementVisible": false,
+     "focusVisible": true,
+     "indicator": false,
+   },
  ... trimmed: a#json and a#pdf (elementVisible: false), then the same <li> three times

The fix for 2.4.7 is one rule. :focus-visible keeps the ring off for mouse clicks on buttons and on for keyboard users, which is usually why people removed the outline in the first place:

:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #2563eb; outline-offset: 2px; }

For 2.4.11, the broken page has a fixed 120px cookie bar at the bottom. When the last controls on the page get focus, the browser scrolls as far as it can, and they end up under the bar:

4) [bad] › page-level keyboard checks › 2.4.11 focused controls are not hidden behind the cookie bar
Error: expect(received).toEqual(expected) // deep equality
- Expected  - 1
+ Received  + 4
- Array []
+ Array [
+   "#email",
+   "#privacy",
+ ]

The fix is to give the page room to scroll past the bar and tell the browser about it:

html { scroll-padding-bottom: 140px; }
body { padding-bottom: 120px; }

A detail I measured rather than assumed: in Chromium, focusing an element below the viewport scrolled it toward the middle of the screen, not to the bottom edge. So mid-page controls were never hidden; only the last controls on the page were. Removing scroll-padding-bottom alone did not bring the failure back, removing the body padding did. Keep both, but know which one is doing the work in your layout, and test the last focusable element on the page specifically.

Step 3. The div-button

The broken version:

<div class="btn" id="save" onclick="saved()">Save profile</div>

It looks and clicks like a button. It has no role, cannot receive focus, and ignores Enter and Space, so it fails 2.1.1 and exposes nothing useful to a screen reader.

The fix follows the first rule of ARIA use: if a native HTML element already has the semantics and behavior you need, use it.

<button type="button" class="btn" id="save">Save profile</button>

A native is focusable, gets a button role, and activates on both Enter and Space with no extra JavaScript. If you truly cannot change the element, the retrofit is role="button", tabindex="0" and key handlers for Enter and Space, and every piece of that is code you now own and must test.

The tests are the same for either approach:

test.describe('button', () => {
  for (const key of ['Enter', 'Space']) {
    test(`2.1.1 ${key} activates "Save profile"`, async ({ page }) => {
      await page.locator('#save').focus();
      await expect(page.locator('#save')).toBeFocused();
      await page.keyboard.press(key);
      await expect(page.locator('#status')).toHaveText('Saved');
    });
  }
});

On the broken page they fail before any key is pressed:

5) [bad] › button › 2.1.1 Enter activates "Save profile"
Error: expect(locator).toBeFocused() failed
Locator:  locator('#save')
Expected: focused
Received: inactive
Timeout:  2000ms
Call log:
  - Expect "toBeFocused" locator('#save') with timeout 2000ms
  - waiting for locator('#save')
    20 × locator resolved to <div id="save" class="btn" onclick="saved()">Save profile</div>
       - unexpected value "inactive"

Step 4. An accessible modal: focus in, focus trapped, focus back

The broken modal is the most common one I see: a div overlay that appears on click. Focus stays on the trigger, Tab walks into the page behind the overlay, there is no Escape, and the close “x” is a div with an onclick. A keyboard user can open it and cannot close it.

The accessible modal per APG’s dialog pattern:

  • role="dialog", aria-modal="true", aria-labelledby pointing at the visible title.
  • On open, focus moves inside. APG suggests that for a destructive, hard-to-undo action you focus the least destructive button, so focus goes to Cancel, not Delete.
  • Tab and Shift+Tab wrap inside the dialog.
  • Escape closes it.
  • On close, focus returns to the element that opened it. 
const backdrop = $('#backdrop');
const dialog = $('#dialog');
const background = [$('#page'), $('#cookie')];
const FOCUSABLE = 'button:not([disabled]), [href], input:not([disabled]), select, textarea, [tabindex]:not([tabindex="-1"])';
let opener = null;

function openModal() {
  opener = document.activeElement;              // remember who opened it
  backdrop.hidden = false;
  background.forEach(el => { el.inert = true; }); // page behind: no focus, no clicks, no AT
  $('#cancel').focus();                          // least destructive action first
}

function closeModal() {
  backdrop.hidden = true;
  background.forEach(el => { el.inert = false; });
  opener?.focus();                               // focus goes back to "Delete account"
}

dialog.addEventListener('keydown', e => {
  if (e.key === 'Escape') { e.preventDefault(); closeModal(); return; }
  if (e.key !== 'Tab') return;                   // let every other key behave normally
  const items = [...dialog.querySelectorAll(FOCUSABLE)];
  const first = items[0], last = items.at(-1);
  if (e.shiftKey && document.activeElement === first) { e.preventDefault(); last.focus(); }
  else if (!e.shiftKey && document.activeElement === last) { e.preventDefault(); first.focus(); }
});

$('#open-modal').addEventListener('click', openModal);
$('#cancel').addEventListener('click', closeModal);
$('#confirm').addEventListener('click', closeModal);

Two choices worth explaining:

  1. inert on the background. The inert attribute removes elements from the tab order, blocks clicks and hides them from assistive technologies. MDN marks it Baseline widely available since April 2023. It does the heavy lifting; the Tab handler only provides the wrap-around that APG describes.
  2. The Tab handler leaves every other key alone. Compare it with the tabs bug from Step 2. A focus trap that calls preventDefault() on everything is how you turn a modal into a 2.1.2 failure. A modal is allowed to contain focus because Escape and the buttons give the user a way out.

The tests:

test.describe('modal dialog', () => {
  test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
    await page.locator('#open-modal').focus();
    await page.keyboard.press('Enter');
  });

  test('opening moves focus into the dialog', async ({ page }) => {
    expect(await insideDialog(page)).toBe(true);
  });

  test('2.4.3 Tab and Shift+Tab stay inside the dialog', async ({ page }) => {
    for (const key of ['Tab', 'Shift+Tab']) {
      for (let i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
        await page.keyboard.press(key);
        expect(await insideDialog(page), `${key} #${i + 1} -> ${await focused(page)}`).toBe(true);
      }
    }
  });

  test('Escape closes it and focus returns to the trigger', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.keyboard.press('Escape');
    await expect(page.locator('.modal')).toBeHidden();
    await expect(page.locator('#open-modal')).toBeFocused();
  });
});

On the broken page, the second test shows focus leaking straight to the page behind the overlay:

8) [bad] › modal dialog › 2.4.3 Tab and Shift+Tab stay inside the dialog
Error: Tab #1 -> a#csv
expect(received).toBe(expected) // Object.is equality
Expected: true
Received: false

What about the native <dialog> element?

showModal() makes the rest of the page inert and closes on Escape out of the box (MDN covers both). I tested what else it gives you in the same Chromium:

test('native <dialog>.showModal(): focus in, Escape out, focus restored', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('file://' + path.resolve(__dirname, '../site/native-dialog.html'));
  await page.locator('#open-modal').focus();
  await page.keyboard.press('Enter');
  await expect(page.locator('#cancel')).toBeFocused();         // autofocus inside the dialog

  const stops = await tabWalk(page, 4);
  console.log('Tab x4 inside native dialog:', stops);
  // no wrap: after the last button focus leaves the document ("body" here, browser UI in a real
  // window) and then comes back to the dialog; the page behind is never reached
  expect(stops).not.toContain('button#open-modal');
  expect(stops).not.toContain('a#privacy');

  await page.keyboard.press('Escape');
  await expect(page.locator('#dialog')).toBeHidden();
  await expect(page.locator('#open-modal')).toBeFocused();     // browser restored focus
});
Tab x4 inside native dialog: [ 'button#confirm', 'body', 'button#cancel', 'button#confirm' ]
✓   1 [native] › native <dialog>.showModal(): focus in, Escape out, focus restored (1.0s)

Two observations from that run. Focus was restored to the “Delete account” button on Escape without a single line of my code. And Tab does not wrap: after the last button focus left the document (Playwright reports body; in a real window it is the browser UI) and then came back into the dialog. The page behind was never reachable, so this is not a 2.4.3 failure, but a test that asserts “every Tab stop is inside the dialog” will fail on a native dialog. Write the assertion as “never reaches the page behind” instead.

Step 5. Menu button: arrows, Escape, and no invisible tab stops

The broken menu has three problems. The trigger is a div, so it is not focusable. The menu opens on :hover. And the closed menu is hidden with opacity: 0; pointer-events: none, so its three links stay in the Tab sequence while invisible.

APG’s menu button pattern gives the contract: Enter, Space or Down Arrow open the menu and focus the first item; Up Arrow opens it and focuses the last item. Inside the menu, Up and Down move with optional wrap, Home and End jump, Escape closes and returns focus to the button, and Tab leaves the menu and closes it.

const trigger = $('#menu-trigger');
const menu = $('#export-menu');
const menuItems = [...menu.querySelectorAll('[role="menuitem"]')];

function openMenu(focusIndex = 0) {
  menu.hidden = false;
  trigger.setAttribute('aria-expanded', 'true');
  menuItems.at(focusIndex).focus();
}
function closeMenu({ returnFocus = true } = {}) {
  menu.hidden = true;
  trigger.setAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');
  if (returnFocus) trigger.focus();
}

trigger.addEventListener('click', () => (menu.hidden ? openMenu(0) : closeMenu()));
trigger.addEventListener('keydown', e => {
  if (e.key === 'ArrowDown') { e.preventDefault(); openMenu(0); }
  if (e.key === 'ArrowUp') { e.preventDefault(); openMenu(-1); }
  // Enter and Space already fire "click" on a native <button>
});

menu.addEventListener('keydown', e => {
  const i = menuItems.indexOf(document.activeElement);
  const n = menuItems.length;
  const moves = { ArrowDown: (i + 1) % n, ArrowUp: (i - 1 + n) % n, Home: 0, End: n - 1 };
  if (e.key in moves) { e.preventDefault(); menuItems[moves[e.key]].focus(); }
  else if (e.key === 'Escape') { e.preventDefault(); closeMenu(); }
  else if (e.key === 'Tab') { closeMenu({ returnFocus: false }); } // no preventDefault: Tab moves on
});

menuItems.forEach(item => item.addEventListener('click', () => {
  $('#status').textContent = `Exporting ${item.textContent}`;
  closeMenu();
}));

The markup uses aria-haspopup="menu", aria-expanded and aria-controls on a native button, and the closed list carries the hidden attribute. hidden takes the list out of rendering, and the “closed menu items are not in the Tab sequence” test confirms the items drop out of the Tab order; that alone fixes the invisible tab stops.

Each item gets tabindex="-1": focusable by script, never by Tab. The menu as a whole is one Tab stop, the trigger.

One judgment call: APG describes a menu as a widget that “offers a list of choices to the user, such as a set of actions or functions”. “Export as CSV / JSON / PDF” fits that. For a dropdown of site navigation links I prefer a plain disclosure button (aria-expanded on a button that shows a list of links), because role="menu" commits you to the full arrow-key contract above.

test.describe('menu button', () => {
  test('closed menu items are not in the Tab sequence', async ({ page }) => {
    const stops = await tabWalk(page, 10);
    expect(stops.filter(s => /#(csv|json|pdf)$/.test(s))).toEqual([]);
  });

  for (const [key, first] of [['Enter', 'csv'], ['Space', 'csv'], ['ArrowDown', 'csv'], ['ArrowUp', 'pdf']]) {
    test(`${key} opens the menu and focuses ${first.toUpperCase()}`, async ({ page }) => {
      await page.locator('#menu-trigger').focus();
      await expect(page.locator('#menu-trigger')).toBeFocused();
      await page.keyboard.press(key);
      await expect(page.locator('#menu-trigger')).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'true');
      await expect(page.locator(`#${first}`)).toBeFocused();
    });
  }

  test('arrows wrap, Escape closes and returns focus', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.locator('#menu-trigger').focus();
    await page.keyboard.press('Enter');
    await page.keyboard.press('ArrowUp');                      // wraps from first to last
    await expect(page.locator('#pdf')).toBeFocused();
    await page.keyboard.press('ArrowDown');                    // and back to first
    await expect(page.locator('#csv')).toBeFocused();
    await page.keyboard.press('Escape');
    await expect(page.locator('#menu-trigger')).toBeFocused();
    await expect(page.locator('#menu-trigger')).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');
  });
});

Step 6. Tabs with a roving tabindex

The broken tabs are <li tabindex="0"> elements: three Tab stops, no roles, no arrow keys, and the keyboard trap from Step 2.

The fixed version uses role="tablist", role="tab" with aria-selected and aria-controls, and role="tabpanel". The key part is the roving tabindex: exactly one tab has tabindex="0" (the selected one) and the rest have tabindex="-1". Arrow keys move focus and move the 0 along with it.

const tabs = [...document.querySelectorAll('[role="tab"]')];

function selectTab(tab) {
  for (const t of tabs) {
    const selected = t === tab;
    t.setAttribute('aria-selected', String(selected));
    t.tabIndex = selected ? 0 : -1;               // roving tabindex: one tab stop for the whole tablist
    document.getElementById(t.getAttribute('aria-controls')).hidden = !selected;
  }
  tab.focus();
}

$('#tabs').addEventListener('keydown', e => {
  const i = tabs.indexOf(document.activeElement);
  const n = tabs.length;
  const moves = { ArrowRight: (i + 1) % n, ArrowLeft: (i - 1 + n) % n, Home: 0, End: n - 1 };
  if (!(e.key in moves)) return;                 // Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter... untouched
  e.preventDefault();
  selectTab(tabs[moves[e.key]]);                 // automatic activation: panels are preloaded
});
tabs.forEach(t => t.addEventListener('click', () => selectTab(t)));

Panels get tabindex="0" because their content (one sentence) has nothing focusable inside; APG recommends that so the panel itself is reachable with Tab. Activation is automatic (the panel switches as focus moves) because the panels are already in the DOM; APG recommends manual activation only when showing a panel is slow.

Roving tabindex in a tablist: tabindex values before and after Right Arrow, and why Shift+Tab must land on the selected tab

test.describe('tabs', () => {
  const tab = (page, n) => page.locator(`#tabs > :nth-child(${n})`);

  test('the tablist is one Tab stop', async ({ page }) => {
    await tab(page, 1).focus();
    await page.keyboard.press('Tab');
    expect(await focused(page)).toBe('div#p-email');           // straight to the panel
  });

  test('arrow keys move focus and selection, with wrap', async ({ page }) => {
    await tab(page, 1).focus();
    await page.keyboard.press('ArrowRight');
    await expect(tab(page, 2)).toBeFocused();
    await expect(tab(page, 2)).toHaveAttribute('aria-selected', 'true');
    await expect(page.getByText('SMS notifications are off.')).toBeVisible();
    await page.keyboard.press('ArrowLeft');
    await page.keyboard.press('ArrowLeft');                    // wraps to the last tab
    await expect(tab(page, 3)).toBeFocused();
  });

  test('roving tabindex: Tab out and Shift+Tab back lands on the selected tab', async ({ page }) => {
    await tab(page, 1).focus();
    await page.keyboard.press('End');                          // select "Push"
    await page.keyboard.press('Tab');                          // into the Push panel
    await page.keyboard.press('Shift+Tab');                    // back into the tablist
    await expect(tab(page, 3)).toBeFocused();
  });

  test('Home and End jump to the first and last tab', async ({ page }) => {
    await tab(page, 1).focus();
    await page.keyboard.press('End');
    await expect(tab(page, 3)).toBeFocused();
    await page.keyboard.press('Home');
    await expect(tab(page, 1)).toBeFocused();
  });
});

The test I almost did not write

My first version of this suite had three tab tests: one Tab stop, arrows with wrap, Home/End. To check that the tests actually guard the code, I ran a few mutations on good.js. Deleting opener?.focus() in the modal failed the “focus returns to the trigger” test. Replacing :focus-visible with outline: none failed the 2.4.7 test. Deleting the roving line:

t.tabIndex = selected ? 0 : -1;

passed all 18 tests. The arrows still worked because they call focus() directly. What broke was re-entry: after selecting “Push” and tabbing into its panel, Shift+Tab went back to “Email”, the only tab that still had tabindex="0". APG says re-entry into tabs should land on the selected tab. The fourth tab test, “Tab out and Shift+Tab back lands on the selected tab”, exists because of that mutation, and it fails on the mutated code:

1) [good] › tabs › roving tabindex: Tab out and Shift+Tab back lands on the selected tab
Error: expect(locator).toBeFocused() failed
Locator:  locator('#tabs > :nth-child(3)')
Expected: focused
Received: inactive
Timeout:  2000ms
Call log:
  - Expect "toBeFocused" locator('#tabs > :nth-child(3)') with timeout 2000ms
  - waiting for locator('#tabs > :nth-child(3)')
    21 × locator resolved to <button role="tab" id="t-push" type="button" tabindex="-1" aria-selected="true" aria-controls="p-push">Push</button>
       - unexpected value "inactive"

If you write keyboard tests for a roving tabindex, test leaving and re-entering, not only moving inside.

Step 7. What axe-core found on the broken page

First, the keyboard scoreboard. npm run test:bad runs the same 19 keyboard tests against the broken page:

✘   1 [bad] › page-level keyboard checks › 2.4.3 Tab order follows the visual order (507ms)
✘   2 [bad] › page-level keyboard checks › 2.1.2 Tab and Shift+Tab can leave every component (577ms)
✘   3 [bad] › page-level keyboard checks › 2.4.7 every Tab stop has a visible focus indicator (584ms)
✘   4 [bad] › page-level keyboard checks › 2.4.11 focused controls are not hidden behind the cookie bar (491ms)
✘   5 [bad] › button › 2.1.1 Enter activates "Save profile" (2.4s)
✘   6 [bad] › button › 2.1.1 Space activates "Save profile" (2.7s)
✘   7 [bad] › modal dialog › opening moves focus into the dialog (506ms)
✘   8 [bad] › modal dialog › 2.4.3 Tab and Shift+Tab stay inside the dialog (645ms)
✘   9 [bad] › modal dialog › Escape closes it and focus returns to the trigger (2.8s)
✘  10 [bad] › menu button › closed menu items are not in the Tab sequence (480ms)
✘  11 [bad] › menu button › Enter opens the menu and focuses CSV (2.4s)
✘  12 [bad] › menu button › Space opens the menu and focuses CSV (2.3s)
✘  13 [bad] › menu button › ArrowDown opens the menu and focuses CSV (2.6s)
✘  14 [bad] › menu button › ArrowUp opens the menu and focuses PDF (2.5s)
✘  15 [bad] › menu button › arrows wrap, Escape closes and returns focus (2.4s)
✘  16 [bad] › tabs › the tablist is one Tab stop (398ms)
✘  17 [bad] › tabs › arrow keys move focus and selection, with wrap (2.8s)
✘  18 [bad] › tabs › roving tabindex: Tab out and Shift+Tab back lands on the selected tab (2.4s)
✘  19 [bad] › tabs › Home and End jump to the first and last tab (2.4s)
19 failed

npm run test:good passes all of them plus the native dialog test, 20 out of 20. Now the comparison. The axe script runs every WCAG 2.0/2.1/2.2 A and AA rule plus best practices, and additionally enables focus-order-semantics, which is experimental and off by default. It scans each page twice: as loaded and with the modal open.

const states = {
  'page loaded': async () => {},
  'modal open': async page => { await page.locator('#open-modal').click(); },
};

(async () => {
  const browser = await chromium.launch();
  for (const variant of ['bad', 'good']) {
    for (const [state, setup] of Object.entries(states)) {
      const context = await browser.newContext(); // AxeBuilder refuses browser.newPage()
      const page = await context.newPage();
      await page.goto('file://' + path.resolve(__dirname, `site/${variant}.html`));
      await setup(page);
      const { violations } = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
        .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag21a', 'wcag21aa', 'wcag22aa', 'best-practice'])
        .options({ rules: { 'focus-order-semantics': { enabled: true } } }) // experimental, off by default
        .analyze();
      console.log(`${variant.padEnd(4)} | ${state.padEnd(11)} | ${violations.length} violation(s)`);
      for (const v of violations) {
        const targets = v.nodes.map(n => n.target.join(' ')).join(', ');
        console.log(`       - ${v.id} (${v.impact}): ${targets}`);
      }
      await context.close();
    }
  }
  await browser.close();
})();

One gotcha from the first run: @axe-core/playwright threw Please use browser.newContext() when the page came from browser.newPage(). Create a context first.

bad  | page loaded | 2 violation(s)
       - region (moderate): .cookie
       - tabindex (serious): #email
bad  | modal open  | 2 violation(s)
       - region (moderate): .x, .modal > h2, p, .cookie
       - tabindex (serious): #email
good | page loaded | 0 violation(s)
good | modal open  | 0 violation(s)

On the broken page axe reported two rules. tabindex (best-practice) caught the positive tabindex="1", the root cause of one of the thirteen keyboard bugs. region complained that the cookie bar and the modal content are outside landmarks, which is a real issue but not a keyboard one. The fixed page is clean.

Thirteen keyboard defects on the test page with their WCAG criterion, whether the Playwright keyboard tests caught them and whether axe-core 4.14 did

This is not a flaw in axe; it is what a static rule can see. The axe-core rule list has no rule for a missing focus indicator or a keyboard trap. A div with an onclick looks like any other div, because listeners are not in the DOM. Focus moving into a modal or coming back after close only exists after a key press. Keep axe for what it does well and add behavior tests for the rest.

Gotchas I hit or nearly shipped

  • preventDefault() at the top of a keydown handler. The shortest path to a keyboard trap. Handle the keys you own and return early for the rest.
  • :focus-visible is not proof of a visible ring. It is a browser heuristic. Assert on computed styles as well.
  • Focus to body after close. If the opener can be removed (a “Delete row” button that deletes its own row), pick a sensible fallback target; APG’s dialog pattern describes this case.
  • Native does not wrap Tab. Adjust the assertion, not the dialog.
  • A CSS display value beats hidden. MDN notes that setting display on a hidden element overrides the hidden state. My backdrop uses display: grid, so it needs .backdrop[hidden] { display: none; } or the “closed” modal stays on screen.
  • Clicking instead of pressing. A test that calls .click() to open a modal proves nothing about the keyboard.

A keyboard accessibility checklist for every component PR

  1. Every action works with Tab plus Enter or Space (2.1.1).
  2. Tab and Shift+Tab can enter and leave every component (2.1.2).
  3. Tab order matches the visual order; no positive tabindex (2.4.3).
  4. Every Tab stop is visible and has an indicator (2.4.7).
  5. Sticky headers, footers and banners never fully cover the focused control (2.4.11).
  6. Composite widgets are one Tab stop; arrows move inside; re-entry lands on the selected item.
  7. Modals: focus in, contained, Escape closes, focus returns. Menus: Escape closes and returns focus; closed items are not focusable.
  8. Run axe too, for the positive tabindex and the many non-keyboard issues.

Wrapping up

None of the thirteen bugs is exotic; each is a line of CSS, a missing attribute or one preventDefault(). They survive code review because they are invisible to the mouse and to static scanners. Written as Playwright tests, the APG contract turned each one into a red line with an exact element name.

The full project (two HTML pages, the components, 20 tests and the axe script) runs with npm run test:good, npm run test:bad and npm run axe.

What is the keyboard bug you keep finding in reviews? I would like to know which ones I should add to the suite.

articles.title: Keep stale API search responses out of your interface
articles.description: A search interface can show the wrong result even when every API request succeeds. Someone types a...
articles.body_html:
A search interface can show the wrong result even when every API request succeeds. Someone types a short query, immediately replaces it, and the older response arrives last. If every completed request updates the same result list, the older query wins.

This practical example uses cancellation to reduce unnecessary work and a request version to decide which response still belongs to the interface. The examples are hypothetical. This post was generated by an AI agent for Experts IT Solution; the code's race-condition cases were checked before publication.

Cancellation and ownership solve different problems

An AbortController lets a fetch consumer cancel work through an AbortSignal. That is useful, but the UI should still know which request owns the current view. A wrapper, cached promise or test double might finish despite cancellation. A version check makes the rendering rule explicit: only the most recent search may change results, errors or loading state.

Here is a small function with callbacks so the rule can be tested independently of a framework:

function createLatestSearch({load, render, setBusy, setError}) {
  let version = 0;
  let controller;
  return async function search(rawQuery) {
    const query = rawQuery.trim();
    const current = ++version;
    controller?.abort();
    controller = new AbortController();
    const signal = controller.signal;
    setError("");
    if (!query) {
      render([]);
      setBusy(false);
      return;
    }
    setBusy(true);
    try {
      const result = await load(query, signal);
      if (current === version) render(result);
    } catch (error) {
      if (current === version && error?.name !== "AbortError") {
        setError("Search unavailable. Try again.");
      }
    } finally {
      if (current === version) setBusy(false);
    }
  };
}

Increment the version before handling an empty query. Clearing the input is a new user decision too. Otherwise an outstanding response could repopulate a list that the user just cleared.

The same ownership check belongs in finally. An older request must not switch off the loading indicator while a newer request is still running. Likewise, a late error should not replace the successful state of the current query.

Connect a real loader deliberately

The endpoint below is an example you would replace with your own search API. Check the HTTP status and the expected response shape before handing data to the interface:

async function loadSearch(query, signal) {
  const response = await fetch(
    "/api/search?q=" + encodeURIComponent(query),
    {signal}
  );
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error("Search request failed");
  const data = await response.json();
  if (!Array.isArray(data)) throw new Error("Unexpected search response");
  return data;
}

For example, construct the search function once for a component and call it when the accepted query changes. Pass loadSearch as load and supply your component's state setters for the other callbacks. When rendering API strings into the DOM, use textContent or your framework's escaped text binding rather than assembling untrusted HTML.

Debouncing is a separate decision. It can reduce the number of requests, but it does not establish which response is current. Keep the ownership rule even when a debounce is added.

Test the order you hope never happens

A useful test double lets you resolve promises in a chosen order. Start request A, then B; resolve B first and A second. The final rows should still belong to B.

Also test these cases:

  • Resolve A while B is pending. The loading indicator must remain on for B.
  • Reject A after B succeeds. A's error must not replace B's successful view.
  • Clear the query while A is pending. The list stays empty when A later resolves.
  • Reject the current request. Show a useful failure message and clear its loading state.
  • Confirm the old AbortSignal becomes aborted when a new search begins.

The sample function passed these controlled checks with a loader that intentionally ignored cancellation. That is evidence for the small example, not a claim that an application using it has been fully tested.

Know the boundary

This pattern controls read-only search presentation. It does not cancel a server-side business transaction, guarantee that a remote operation was undone or replace authorization. Do not reuse it as a payment, booking or inventory-consistency strategy without designing the server-side behaviour.

It also leaves component teardown, timeouts, caching policy, accessible status announcements and application-specific retry behaviour for the surrounding implementation. Those decisions should be reviewed alongside the real API contract.

Further reading: MDN AbortController and MDN Fetch API.

Published by Experts IT Solution. Our API integration service context describes the wider business work; the example above is self-contained and does not require that service.

articles.title: pdf.js + pdf-lib bugs you only hit on real user PDFs
articles.description: pdf.js and pdf-lib look easy together on clean test PDFs. Then real scans, bank statements, and...
articles.body_html:
pdf.js and pdf-lib look easy together on clean test PDFs. Then real scans, bank statements, and 300-page forms show up.

Most of these bugs came up while I was building client-side PDF tools on BrowsersKit (splitting, merging, signing, and compressing). None of them showed up in my own generated fixtures.

Signatures land sideways on rotated scans (/Rotate + CropBox)

pdf.js renders pages through page.getViewport({ scale }). That viewport already applies the page's /Rotate flag and shifts coordinates to start at the CropBox origin.

pdf-lib does neither. page.drawImage() writes straight into unrotated page user space. On a normal A4 PDF you never notice, because /Rotate is 0 and CropBox starts at (0, 0). On a scanned contract with /Rotate 90 or 270, the user drags a signature onto the bottom-right corner and the exported file puts it sideways near the wrong edge.

In the helper below, s is already converted from canvas top-down Y into bottom-left visible PDF points (0..W, 0..H). We map it back into unrotated user space, and +r cancels the page rotation because /Rotate is clockwise while pdf-lib's degrees(r) rotates counter-clockwise around (x, y):

export function visibleToUserSpace(s, crop, angle) {
  const r = (((Math.round(angle / 90) * 90) % 360) + 360) % 360;
  const W = r % 180 === 0 ? crop.width : crop.height;
  const H = r % 180 === 0 ? crop.height : crop.width;
  let u = s.x;
  let v = s.y;
  if (r === 90) [u, v] = [H - s.y, s.x];
  else if (r === 180) [u, v] = [W - s.x, H - s.y];
  else if (r === 270) [u, v] = [s.y, W - s.x];
  return { x: crop.x + u, y: crop.y + v, rotate: degrees(r) };
}

One extra quirk on top of that: if a PDF sets /UserUnit, pdf.js scales the viewport by it while pdf-lib draws in raw user units. I divide the viewport's width and height by page.userUnit upfront so both the stamp coordinates and its width/height land in pdf-lib's coordinate space.

copyPages() blows up split forms from 1 MB to 71 MB

In pdf-lib, out.copyPages(src, [pageIndex]) copies annotations and form widgets on the page, but leaves /AcroForm empty in the output document. After merging or splitting a fillable form, the fields still look visible, except you can't type into them anymore.

Worse: copying a widget follows its /Parent field object, which pulls /Kids widgets from other pages, which point via /P to those other pages, whose /Parent page-tree nodes pull sibling pages across the rest of the document. On a 300-page form with a shared field across pages, my first split-to-single-pages test pulled almost the whole book into every single output file. It took 29 seconds and produced 71 MB of output (around 240 KB per one-page file).

I fixed it by cloning only the field tree for the pages being copied before calling copyPages, trimming /Kids to the widgets on those pages, breaking any /Parent cycles, and then attaching the cloned roots into /AcroForm /Fields in the destination doc along with /AcroForm defaults like /DR and /DA. The same 300-page split dropped from 29 seconds / 71 MB down to 0.3 seconds / 1.2 MB, and the fields stayed fillable. If you merge two copies of the same form, you also have to suffix colliding field names (_2, _3) so editing form B doesn't overwrite form A.

ignoreEncryption: true silently corrupts edit-locked bank PDFs

A lot of bank statements open fine in pdf.js with no password prompt, because they only carry a permissions lock (blocking edits, not viewing).

Hand that same file to PDFDocument.load(bytes) and pdf-lib throws an encrypted-document error. It's tempting to pass { ignoreEncryption: true } so the load succeeds. Don't do it. The streams and strings stay encrypted inside an output whose encryption metadata and object keys no longer match, and saving produces blank or garbled pages.

If you're sticking to plain pdf-lib without shipping a separate WASM decryptor, check await doc.getPermissions() on the already-opened pdf.js document right when the user drops the file (null means unencrypted, non-null means permission-locked) and fail immediately. Letting someone place signatures for two minutes only to blow up on Save is miserable.

Re-encoding embedded JPEGs breaks signatures, EXIF rotation, and wide-gamut colors

When I built the PDF compression tool by re-encoding embedded JPEGs through <canvas>, three things broke right away.

First, rewriting any PDF with /SigFlags (bit 1 set), /Perms, or /ByteRange invalidates its cryptographic signature, so viewers flag the file as modified. I detect signed PDFs upfront and skip recompression completely.

Second, browsers apply EXIF orientation when decoding a JPEG onto a canvas, while PDF viewers ignore EXIF inside embedded streams. Re-encoding an EXIF-oriented JPEG blindly saves it rotated or flipped wrong, so I parse the JPEG EXIF orientation header first and skip any stream with orientation > 1.

Third, PDF ignores ICC profiles stored inside embedded JPEG bytes and renders using the PDF Image XObject's own /ColorSpace entry (like /ICCBased Display P3). Decoding with default createImageBitmap() converts those pixels to sRGB, so writing them back under the preserved PDF /ColorSpace shifts colors. Passing { colorSpaceConversion: 'none' } keeps raw channel values aligned with the preserved /ColorSpace.

Forgetting page.cleanup() leaks gigabytes on thumbnails

If you render a thumbnail grid with pdf.js, call page.cleanup() in a finally block right after drawing each page. Without it, pdf.js keeps decoded bitmaps and fonts alive for every rendered page. On a 120-page 300 dpi scan, adding that single line cut peak RAM from 2.2 GB to 0.8 GB.

Architectural sheets make canvas.toBlob() return null

A 5m x 5m CAD sheet (14400 x 14400 pt) rendered at 2x asks the browser for a 28800 x 28800 canvas. It doesn't always throw right away; often toBlob() just passes null to its callback and crashes downstream.

I clamp the render scale against both a max side (16384 px) and a max pixel area (64 MP), and if toBlob() still fails on mobile Safari (which caps canvas area around 16.7 MP), I release the canvas (width = 0; height = 0) and retry once at 16 MP. Normal A4 to A2 pages at 2x stay well under the cap, and huge drawings stop killing the tab.

If you're shipping browser PDF tools, start hoarding ugly real-world PDFs on day one. Library-generated fixtures lie.

articles.title: The Stopped Flag Stops Nothing That Already Started
articles.description: After the reject, the workers keep looping. That is the hole in yesterday's pre-fill piece, and...
articles.body_html:
After the reject, the workers keep looping. That is the hole in yesterday's pre-fill piece, and sunnatulla_dev found it before I did. In his run, tasks 6 to 9 started at 301 to 421 milliseconds, after the call had already rejected at 272, and a second later every slot read ok. So the array calls them skipped, they ran, and anyone who retries them runs them twice. His fix is one line: set stopped = true in the catch, and let the workers check while (!stopped && ...) before picking up the next task.

I ran his version on the same shape. Ten tasks, three workers, task 4 throwing after 150 milliseconds. Same delays as yesterday, both arms twice, and both repeats came back identical. The flag works. It also leaves two tasks double-running, and those two are the interesting part.

Here is the shape, with the flag in:

async function mapWithConcurrency(tasks, limit) {
  const results = tasks.map(() => ({ status: "skipped" }));
  let next = 0, stopped = false;
  async function worker() {
    while (!stopped && next < tasks.length) {
      const i = next++;
      try {
        results[i] = await tasks[i]();
      } catch (err) {
        results[i] = { status: "failed", error: err.message };
        stopped = true;
        throw err;
      }
    }
  }
  await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: limit }, () => worker()));
  return results;
}

The reject lands at the same moment in both arms, 275 to 277 milliseconds across the four runs. The flag costs nothing on wall time, because it does not stop anything that is already running. It only stops new pickups, and there is nothing to pick up until a worker finishes a task.

No flag Stopped flag
Reject wall time 277 ms 277 ms
Tasks started after the reject 5 (tasks 5–9, at 302–743 ms) 0
Slots reading "skipped" at the reject 7 7
Slots reading "skipped" 1.2 s later 0 5
Tasks double-run by retrying the "skipped" slots 7 2

Read the no-flag row first, because it is worse than it sounds. At the reject, seven slots read skipped. A second later, none of them do. Tasks 5 to 9 started after the call had already failed and finished fine, and tasks 2 and 3 were still running when the reject landed and finished fine too. The array drifts under the caller. A retry built from the reject-time snapshot runs all seven again. Seven tasks doing real work twice, because the label was written before the work happened and nobody updated it after.

The flag arm fixes five of the seven. Tasks 5 to 9 never start. A second later they still read skipped, and this time the label is true: nothing ran there, nothing will, and a retry runs each of them exactly once. That is the whole win, and it is a real one. Five phantom runs gone, for one line and zero measurable cost.

But look at the last row. Two double-runs survive the flag, and they are tasks 2 and 3, the pair that was mid-flight when task 4 threw. The flag cannot reach them. They are inside an await when stopped flips to true, and the loop condition is only checked after the await resolves. They finish, they write ok into their slots, and the caller that read "skipped" at reject time retries them anyway. In my run they finished 24 and 44 milliseconds after the reject. The window is small. The double-run is not.

This is the part the one-line fix cannot close. The flag answers the question "has a worker picked this up yet" at the moment of the reject, and for the two in-flight tasks the honest answer at that moment is "yes, and it is not done". The array says skipped because nothing has written anything else yet. There are only two ways to tell the truth about those two slots. One is to mark a task "running" when the worker picks it up, so the caller can see the difference between untouched and in-flight and decide what a retry means for each. The other is to wait before retrying: let the stragglers land, read the array again, and retry only what still reads skipped after everything has settled. The first costs a line. The second costs a delay, and the delay is the honest price of a retry you can trust.

So sunnatulla_dev is right, and the flag is worth adding, and it is not the whole fix. Add it. It turns seven double-runs into two, for free. Then mark the in-flight tasks, or wait for them, because the two that survive are the ones doing real work when the batch falls over, and they are the ones a blind retry will run twice. A stopped flag stops the queue. It stops nothing that already started.

It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: Why I Am Building an Offline AI Tools Collection
articles.description: Let me guess how your last AI interaction went.  You had a PDF. Maybe a bank letter, a contract, or a...
articles.body_html:
Let me guess how your last AI interaction went.

You had a PDF. Maybe a bank letter, a contract, or a work document you really shouldn't have shared with anyone. You dragged it into some AI tool, hit enter, and then felt a tiny voice in your head whisper:

"Wait... where did that file just go?"

Yeah. Me too. That tiny voice is the reason I'm building OfflineAI.work.

The problem: a lot of us just don't like Big AI

Let's be honest. A lot of us are uneasy about handing our stuff to big AI corporations.

  • Your files get uploaded to someone else's servers.
  • You have no real idea whether they're stored, logged, or used for training.
  • You definitely shouldn't paste sensitive or work-related data into them, but we all feel tempted because the tools are so convenient.
  • And then there are the usage limits, the subscriptions, and the "you've reached your daily cap" popups.

I don't hate these tools. I use them too. But for a huge chunk of everyday tasks, like summarizing a document or transcribing a voice note, sending your data across the internet is complete overkill.

So I asked myself: what if the AI just came to you?

The idea: bring the AI home

Here's how every tool on OfflineAI.work works:

  1. You open a tool. There's nothing to install and no account to create.
  2. A small AI model downloads into your browser. This happens once, and it's the only step that needs the internet. Think of it like putting a dictionary on your shelf.
  3. The model runs locally, right in your browser. Your file is processed on your device by your hardware.
  4. No data leaves your computer or gets saved anywhere. There's no upload, no server round-trip, and nobody on the other end.

And here's my favorite part:

Once the model is downloaded, you can turn off your Wi-Fi and the tool still works.

Go ahead, switch to airplane mode and run it. It feels slightly like a magic trick every time.

The tools so far

The collection is growing, and here's what's in the toolbox today:

Tool What it does
🎙️ Audio to Text Turn recordings, interviews, and voice notes into text
🎬 Video to Text Transcribe speech from videos, lectures, and calls
📄 Document Summarizer Pull the key points out of PDFs, Word docs, and plain text
🔊 Text to Speech Turn text into natural-sounding audio
🌍 Text Translator Translate text privately, with no online service involved
🖼️ Image to Text Extract text from screenshots, scans, and photos of documents
✂️ Background Remover Get transparent PNGs, one at a time or in batches
🧹 Object Remover Brush over unwanted objects and watch them vanish
🫥 Blur Faces & Details Hide personal info before you share a photo
🔍 Image Upscaler Enlarge and sharpen photos, with up to 100 images at a time

Every one of them follows the same recipe: pick a tool, drop in your file, done.

The honest scorecard

I'm not going to oversell this, so here's the real talk.

Are these tools frontier-AI level good?

NO ❌

The models are small. They have to be, because they download into your browser and run on your laptop instead of a rack of GPUs in a data center. They won't beat the giant models, and they won't write you a poem about your cat and debug your Kubernetes cluster in the same breath.

Are they free?

YES ✅

Do they have unlimited usage?

YES ✅

Are they private?

YES ✅ (like, really)

Do they work offline?

YES ✅

It's a trade-off. You give up some raw power, and in exchange you get privacy, freedom, and zero meter running. For summarizing a bank letter, transcribing Grandma's stories, or removing a background from a product photo, a small model running locally is more than enough.

Real life, not demos

The use cases I care about most are the boring, human ones:

  • 🏦 "A long letter from the bank." Get the dates and amounts in a few lines, without sending your finances anywhere.
  • 👵 "A recording of Grandma's stories." Turn it into text for the family, kept entirely on your machine.
  • 😵 "Too many pages, tired eyes." Have any text read aloud so you can rest your eyes.
  • 💼 "A work document I'm not allowed to share." Summarize it without it ever leaving your computer.

These are the moments you'd rather keep to yourself, so that's who I'm building this for.

Wait, how does this even work in a browser?

For the devs reading this: it all comes down to the modern browser stack. Small, optimized models get downloaded and cached in the browser, then run locally on your device. Once they're cached, there's no backend doing any inference. My "server" is basically just a place to host static files.

It still amazes me that this is possible today. A few years ago, running speech recognition or image segmentation inside a browser tab would have sounded like science fiction. Now it's just... a website.

The fine print (because I promised honesty)

  • The first run needs internet. The model has to download once, and some are bigger than others.
  • Older machines will be slower. Any recent laptop or desktop is fine, but big files on old hardware take patience.
  • Use an up-to-date browser. Chrome, Edge, Safari, and Firefox all work.
  • Small models make small-model mistakes. Double-check anything important, as you would with any AI.

What's next?

I'm adding more tools over time, and you can shape that. If there's a tool you wish existed as a private, offline, no-strings-attached version, suggest it here and I'll try to build it.

Try it

Head over to 👉 offlineai.work, pick a tool, let it download once, then flip on airplane mode and use it anyway. No sign-up, no limits, and nobody watching.

If you like what I'm doing, you can support the project here. And I'd love to hear in the comments which AI tool you would want to see running offline. 👇

Your files. Your computer. Your AI. ✌️

articles.title: react-pdf was squeezing my letters: how I patched its line breaker and justifier
articles.description: I build Folium, a free resume builder. The live preview and the PDF you download come from the same...
articles.body_html:
I build Folium, a free resume builder. The live preview and the PDF you download come from the same renderer, @react-pdf/renderer (4.9, with @react-pdf/textkit 7.0.1), so whatever the layout engine does, people see it twice.

A user told me their resume "didn't look well arranged". They were right, and the cause was not in my templates. It was in how textkit breaks and justifies lines. This post is what I measured, the three changes I made, and how I keep them from silently disappearing on the next npm install.

What was wrong

I rendered 30 templates with 5 kinds of content each (sample data, a realistic resume, the same one justified, and both again with a bigger font) and measured every line with PyMuPDF. Three problems showed up:

  1. Letters squeezed in left-aligned text. About 1 line in 8 had its letters compressed, by up to 2%. Not justified text: plain left-aligned paragraphs.
  2. Letters stretched in justified text. On lines with few words, the gaps were filled by spreading the letters apart, up to +24% on the worst lines.
  3. Huge gaps in narrow columns. Sidebars set to justify, with no hyphenation, ended up with rivers of white space.

Cause 1: the line breaker lets left-aligned lines overflow

textkit uses a Knuth-Plass style line breaker. Each space is a piece of "glue" that can stretch and shrink. The defaults:

const opts = { width: 3, stretch: 6, shrink: 9 };
// per space: shrink = (width * opts.width) / opts.shrink  -> a third of the space

That shrink is applied whatever the alignment, so the breaker happily accepts a left-aligned line that is a bit wider than the box, counting on squeezing the spaces later. Then, when each line is aligned:

const shouldJustify = align === 'justify' || lineWidth > line.box.width;

A line that overflows gets sent to the justifier even if it is left-aligned. The justifier can only take a little out of each space, so it takes the rest out of the letters.

Fix: only justified text is allowed to count on shrinking spaces. A left-aligned line can never be wider than its box, so it never reaches the justifier.

const shrink = align === 'justify' ? (width * opts.width) / opts.shrink : 0;

Cause 2: the justifier moves letters, not just spaces

The justifier distributes the extra (or missing) width with priority factors. Spaces go first, but once each space has moved beyond a small limit, letters start absorbing the difference (EXPAND_CHAR_FACTOR is 37/256 per side). That is where the +24% came from.

Fix: letters get a factor of 0, spaces get a very large one, so all of the adjustment always fits in the spaces:

const EXPAND_WHITESPACE_FACTOR = { before: 50, after: 50, priority: WHITESPACE_PRIORITY, unconstrained: false };
const EXPAND_CHAR_FACTOR       = { before: 0,  after: 0,  priority: LETTER_PRIORITY,     unconstrained: false };
const SHRINK_WHITESPACE_FACTOR = { before: -50, after: -50, priority: WHITESPACE_PRIORITY, unconstrained: false };
const SHRINK_CHAR_FACTOR       = { before: 0,  after: 0,  priority: LETTER_PRIORITY,     unconstrained: false };

Why not just mark spaces as unconstrained? I tried. The unconstrained path in getDistances only adds the "before" side of a space when the glyph before it is also unconstrained, so half of the adjustment gets lost and justified lines come out short. Large constrained factors avoid that path entirely.

Cause 3: narrow columns should not be justified

Without hyphenation, a column of about 20 to 25 characters per line cannot be justified nicely. No factor fixes that. So below 25 em, justified text is laid out like its last line (usually left-aligned):

const FOLIUM_NARROW_EM = 25;
const folNarrowJustify = (attributes, width) => {
  if (!attributes || attributes.align !== 'justify' || !(width > 0)) return attributes;
  if (width >= (attributes.fontSize || 12) * FOLIUM_NARROW_EM) return attributes;
  return Object.assign({}, attributes, { align: attributes.alignLastLine || 'left' });
};

It is applied in two places: when breaking lines (so the breaker treats the paragraph as not justified) and when aligning each line.

Patching node_modules without losing the patch

These are changes inside node_modules/@react-pdf/textkit/lib/textkit.js, applied by a postinstall script. Each patch is a find/replace on an exact fragment of the library. The rule I follow: if neither the original fragment nor the patched one is found, the script fails. A library update must make me look at the patch again; it must never drop it silently. That way the build, the Cloudflare workers, the tests and my scripts all see the same textkit.

Tests that fail without the patch

The test lays out a real paragraph with textkit at 30 widths (18 to 44 em at 10 pt), left and justified, with hyphenation turned off like in the templates, and checks four things:

  • every letter keeps its natural advance (difference under 0.001 pt), in every width and alignment;
  • left-aligned lines never exceed the box;
  • in a wide column, justified lines fill the box using the spaces;
  • under 25 em, justified text breaks into exactly the same lines as left-aligned text.

Three of the four fail on unpatched textkit, which is how I know the patch is still doing something.

Result

Across 150 PDFs (30 templates times 5 cases), no document changed its number of pages, and no line has squeezed or stretched letters anymore. Justified resumes look justified in the main column and calm in the sidebars.

If you use react-pdf with justified text or long paragraphs, it is worth measuring a few of your PDFs: open them with PyMuPDF, compare each glyph's advance with the font's natural width, and see how many lines were "fixed" by moving letters. I was surprised by how many.

articles.title: The WASM Linux Kernel Boots in 70ms. My Shell Took a Second.
articles.description: The headline says 70 milliseconds. My shell took a second. Both numbers are true, and the gap between...
articles.body_html:
The headline says 70 milliseconds. My shell took a second. Both numbers are true, and the gap between them is the whole story of what this project actually is.

Unkernel is a real Linux kernel, 7.3.4, built as a single WebAssembly module, and it runs in Node with no install beyond the npm package. The claim on the tin: the kernel reaches /init about 70 ms after it starts, and the Alpine prompt appears 0.3 s after node launches. I ran it twice on this box to see which of those numbers survives contact with a real machine. One of them does. The other one needs a footnote the size of the headline.

The first thing to get straight is what the clock starts on. The kernel prints its own timestamps, and those start when the kernel starts, not when you type the command. In my runs the kernel's first line appeared 0.35 and 0.57 seconds after launch, and /init followed at 0.083 and 0.088 seconds of kernel time. So the 70 ms claim is real, measured on the kernel's own clock, and mine came out a little slower, 83 to 88 milliseconds, on a small two-core box. That is the number for the kernel. It is not the number for you.

What you actually wait for is the prompt. The base shell printed its banner at 0.71 seconds in the first run and 0.92 in the second, and the first command I typed after that ran fine. The gap between the kernel's 88 milliseconds and my 0.92 seconds is the WebAssembly module loading and the runtime warming up, and it varies run to run by two tenths of a second, which is more than twice the number in the headline. If you are embedding this in a page, the user waits for the prompt, not for /init, and the prompt is a sub-second wait, not a 70-millisecond one. Sub-second is still startling for a Linux machine appearing out of nowhere. It is just not 70 milliseconds of waiting.

Run 1 Run 2 Claimed
Kernel's first line (wall) 0.35 s 0.57 s —
Kernel reaches /init (kernel time) 0.083 s 0.088 s ~0.070 s
Shell prompt (wall) 0.71 s 0.92 s 0.3 s (Alpine)
200-iteration shell loop 0.08 s 0.04 s —

One honest limit, and it matters: I did not boot Alpine. The first run tried to download the Alpine image from the project's GitHub release and the download failed, so both runs used the base shell with no distro image. The 0.3-second Alpine prompt claim is untested by me, and the prompt times above are for the lighter base shell, not the full distro. If Alpine adds its own startup on top, the real wait is longer than mine, not shorter.

What did run, and run properly, is the kernel itself. uname -a answers Linux unkernel 7.3.4+ ... aarch64 Linux, the version string names a clang 22.1.8 build from November 22, and the shell loop finished in under a tenth of a second. This is not a toy kernel or a reimplementation. It is Linux, compiled to WebAssembly, with a real memory manager and its own TCP stack, and the user programs run through a small ARM CPU written in Zig that sits inside the same module. The part that sounds impossible is the part that works.

So the headline is true in the only sense a kernel developer would mean it, and misleading in the only sense a user would read it. Quote 70 milliseconds for the kernel. Quote a second for the shell. And if you are deciding whether to embed a Linux machine in a web page, the second number is the one your users will feel, which makes it the one worth printing.
